## ACL 2022 Best Paper Award Winner

The **Best Paper Award** at ACL 2022 went to:

**"Learned Incremental Representations for Parsing"** by Nikita Kitaev, Thomas Lu, and Dan Klein

This paper was published in the Proceedings of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 3086–3095, Dublin, Ireland, in May 2022.

**Key details:**
- **ACL Anthology ID:** 2022.acl-long.220
- **DOI:** 10.18653/v1/2022.acl-long.220
- **URL:** https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.220/
- The paper's award designation in the ACL Anthology metadata is listed as 'Best Paper'.

**About the paper:** The authors present an incremental syntactic representation that consists of assigning a single discrete label to each word in a sentence, where the label is predicted using strictly incremental processing of a prefix of the sentence, and the sequence of labels for a sentence fully determines a parse tree. They also provide an analysis of the representations learned by their system, investigating properties such as the interpretable syntactic features captured by the system and mechanisms for deferred resolution of syntactic ambiguities.

**Selection process:** From the committed ACL 2022 papers, 32 were selected as candidates for Best Paper awards based on nominations by the Senior Area Chairs, including Best Research Paper, Best Special Theme Paper, Best Resource Paper, and Best Linguistic Insight Paper categories. These papers were assessed by the Best Paper Award Committee. The selected best papers were presented in a dedicated plenary session for Best Paper Awards on May 24, 2022.

## Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList

**Authors:** Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Tongshuang Wu, Carlos Guestrin, and Sameer Singh

**Award:** Best Overall Paper at ACL 2020

**ACL Anthology Link:** https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.442/

**Publication Details:** Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, July 2020, pages 4902–4912. DOI: 10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.442

### Summary

The Best Overall Paper went to "Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList" by researchers from Microsoft, University of Washington, and University of California-Irvine.

The paper addresses a key gap in NLP evaluation: a single aggregate statistic like accuracy makes it difficult to estimate where a model is failing and how to fix it, and alternative evaluation approaches usually focus on individual tasks or specific capabilities.

To address this, the authors introduce CheckList, a task-agnostic methodology for testing NLP models inspired by principles of behavioral testing in software engineering. CheckList includes a matrix of general linguistic capabilities and test types that facilitate comprehensive test ideation, as well as a software tool to generate a large and diverse number of test cases quickly.

### Key Findings

- The authors illustrate the utility of CheckList with tests for three tasks, identifying critical failures in both commercial and state-of-art models.
- In a user study, a team responsible for a commercial sentiment analysis model found new and actionable bugs in an extensively tested model.
- In another user study, NLP practitioners with CheckList created twice as many tests, and found almost three times as many bugs as users without it.

### Honorable Mentions at ACL 2020

The honourable mentions were "Don't Stop Pretraining: Adapt Language Models to Domains and Tasks" by researchers from the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence and University of Washington; and "Tangled up in BLEU: Reevaluating the Evaluation of Automatic Machine Translation Evaluation Metrics" by researchers from the University of Melbourne.

### Context

A total of 779 papers (571 long papers and 208 short papers) were selected by the ACL conference committee that year from 3,088 submissions — an acceptance rate of 25.2 percent. Originally scheduled for Seattle in the US, ACL 2020 was moved online due to the COVID-19 pandemic and ran July 5 to 10.

## Paper Details

**Title:** Vocabulary Learning via Optimal Transport for Neural Machine Translation

**Authors:** Jingjing Xu, Hao Zhou, Chun Gan, Zaixiang Zheng, and Lei Li

**Publication:** In Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 7361–7373, Online

**ACL Anthology Link:** https://aclanthology.org/2021.acl-long.571/

## About the Research

The ACL 2021 best paper honours went to a team from ByteDance AI Lab, University of Wisconsin–Madison and Nanjing University. Their paper treats vocabulary construction for machine translation, aka vocabularization, as an optimal transport (OT) problem, and proposes VOLT (Vocabulary Learning via Optimal Transport), a simple and efficient approach that works without trial training.

The performance of neural machine translation (NMT) systems is highly dependent on the choice of token vocabularies, and so it is crucial to identify a good vocabulary and find the optimal tokens — a process that typically involves intensive and laborious trial training.

## Significance

The best paper is selected from 3350 submissions to ACL 2021, the leading conference on natural language processing. This paper explores an optimal and efficient vocabulary learning algorithm VOLT, without expensive trial training, for improved performance in machine translation. The conducted experiments affirmed VOLT's ability to effectively find good vocabulary 100 times faster than traditional approaches across diverse scenarios, which can ultimately enhance machine translation performance.

## Resources

- **ACL Anthology:** https://aclanthology.org/2021.acl-long.571/
- **PDF:** https://aclanthology.org/2021.acl-long.571.pdf
- **arXiv:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.15671
- **Code:** Available at https://github.com/Jingjing-NLP/VOLT
